title: Stylos: Single-Forward 3D Stylization
one_liner: A single-forward method that takes a content scene and style image, then applies artistic style uniformly across all viewpoints without retraining.
lead: Style transfer on 3D scenes usually requires retraining the model for each scene. Stylos instead uses a transformer that splits into two pathways: one pathway predicts where each 3D point should be located and how bright it is before styling, while the other pathway blends in the artistic style. A special loss keeps the style consistent across different camera angles while preserving the original shape.

problem.h2: Why old 3D style transfer is stuck
paras: To stylize a 3D scene (make it look painted or sketched), old methods required you to optimize a separate model for every single scene, which is slow and fragile. You also needed the exact camera positions (poses) beforehand, which is not always available. A beginner might try: take a style image, run a style loss on each rendered view, and hope the results stay consistent. This breaks because each view trains independently, so the same shape gets styled differently from different angles, creating a patchwork effect.

The core problem is that views compete: if you stylize view A to match the style image, then view B of the same object ends up with conflicting surface patterns. The predicted positions and colors of each 3D point start to warp to satisfy both views, ruining the shape.

callout.html: Stylos uses a transformer with two separate pathways: one pathway keeps the predicted 3D positions and base colors locked in place by attending to local neighborhoods, while a second pathway injects style information globally across all views at once, enforced by a 3D loss that compares aggregated features in voxel space instead of view by view.

panels.title: 1. The input: a content scene and a reference style.
panels.caption: A 3D shape (e.g. a statue) and an artistic style (oil painting).

panels.title: 2. Old method: each view trains alone, styles conflict.
panels.caption: Each camera angle optimizes independently; the same surface gets different colors.

panels.title: 3. Stylos splits shape and style.
panels.caption: Shape pathway stays put; style pathway pulls all views together.

panels.title: 4. Voxel loss: compare style in 3D, not per image.
panels.caption: Features from all views fuse into a 3D grid; style is enforced at that level.

panels.title: 5. Result: consistent style, shape preserved.
panels.caption: All viewpoints show the same style on the same surfaces.

steps.text: Content scene and style reference go through a shared feature extractor.
Shape path attends to nearby pixels in the same view to preserve structure; style path pulls artistic cues from the reference to all views.
Style embeddings are assigned to each 3D point (Gaussian) based on both shape and style features.
All rendered views contribute their features to a shared 3D voxel grid, so conflicts between views dissolve.
The loss compares aggregated voxel features to style statistics; a mismatch nudges training toward consistency.

paras: Stylos replaces per-view, per-scene training with a single transformer run that takes unposed images as input. Instead of optimizing a neural field for hours per scene, the model immediately predicts 3D point locations, brightness, and style properties. The key shift is that training happens once on a dataset, then the model generalizes to brand-new scenes and styles when answering questions about new images (inference).

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: View-consistent style encoding
hidden.name: voxel style coherence
paras: The paper measures how much the style is consistent across viewpoints. This is not a single number on each image; instead, it is a comparison of feature statistics in 3D voxel space. Every voxel (a small cube in the 3D scene) collects features from all camera angles that can see it. If those features match the pattern of colors and textures in the style reference, the voxel is styled. If they do not, the loss penalizes the discrepancy.

The paper estimates voxel coherence by rendering the scene from many angles, extracting deep features (from a pretrained vision model) for each rendered view, then fusing all those features into a single 3D grid. It then computes the mean and standard deviation (the statistics) of features in that grid and compares them to the style image's feature statistics.

heat.caption: Darker cells indicate stronger voxel-level style coherence. Highlighted voxels show where multi-view fusion enforces consistency.

reads.html: To know if all camera angles agree on the style, look at the features they produce for the same 3D location. If they all predict similar colors and textures, the style is consistent.
The paper defines the 3D style loss L_sty as the sum of squared differences between the mean and variance of VGG features in the voxelized scene and the style reference, weighted by layer.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: the causal chain
paras: The core problem is that if you optimize each view independently, they pull the predicted 3D points in conflicting directions. Stylos breaks this by forcing shape and style to be computed in separate pathways within the same transformer.

The shape pathway uses local neighborhood attention, which means each location attends to nearby pixels in the same view to predict its position and brightness. This local reasoning preserves the original structure. The style pathway uses global cross-attention, which means style information is pulled from the reference image and sent to all views at once. Because it is global, the same artistic signal reaches every view, eliminating conflicts.

The voxel loss seals the deal. Instead of comparing each view's rendering to the style (which reopens conflicts), the method aggregates all view features into a single 3D grid and compares that grid to style statistics. Because the loss operates on fused 3D data, not per-view 2D images, there is nowhere for view conflicts to hide. The training nudges features toward a single coherent pattern of colors and textures.

stages.s: Unposed scene images and style reference
Shape path: attend to neighbors in each view
Style path: pull artistic cues to all views
Assign style embeddings to each 3D point
Render from many angles and extract deep features
Compare voxel statistics to style reference

math.words: The 3D style loss sums, over multiple feature layers, the squared distance between the mean features of the voxelized scene and the style reference, plus the squared distance between their variances.
math.equation: L_sty_3D = (1/B) * sum_b sum_l alpha_l * (||mean(G_b_l) - mean(S_l)||^2 + ||variance(G_b_l) - variance(S_l)||^2)
symbols: number of scenes in a batch
layer index in the feature extractor (e.g. layer 1 through 5 of a vision model)
weight for layer l, controls how much that layer contributes
feature map of the scene b at layer l, aggregated in voxel space
feature map of the style reference image at layer l
average value of features across all voxels
spread of features (how different they are from the average)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose layer 3 has alpha_3 = 1.0. Scene voxels have mean color brightness 0.6, style reference has mean 0.5. Difference: 0.6 - 0.5 = 0.1. Squared: 0.01.
Scene voxels have color variance (spread) 0.08, style has 0.12. Difference: 0.08 - 0.12 = -0.04. Squared: 0.0016.
Layer 3 contributes 1.0 * (0.01 + 0.0016) = 0.0116 to the loss. Multiple layers sum up.
When loss is large, training adjusts the scene features. When loss shrinks, voxel style coherence is achieved.

math.note: The loss penalizes both mean and variance mismatches, so training makes the voxel features match the style not just in average brightness, but in how varied they are across the 3D space.

charts.title: Per-view style loss (old approach)
charts.note: Each view trains independently, so some match the style well and others poorly. 3D points warp due to conflicting pressure.

charts.title: Voxel 3D style loss (Stylos)
charts.note: All views achieve similar style accuracy because the loss operates on aggregated 3D features. Shape is preserved because it has a dedicated pathway.

items.b: Weak shape signal in the content images.
items.html: If the input images are blurry or poorly lit, the shape pathway cannot predict accurate 3D positions and base colors. The stylized result will look distorted.

items.b: Style reference does not match the content well.
items.html: If the reference style is, say, a sepia tone and the content is a bright neon scene, the voxel features may be pulled in directions that hurt visual quality. The method does what it is told, not what looks best.

items.b: Small numbers of viewpoints in the input.
items.html: With only one or two images, the shape prediction has little information to infer 3D positions and scales. Voxel aggregation cannot fuse consistent features from a single angle.

items.b: Shape and style pathways balance well.
items.html: When the shape pathway is strong and the style loss weights are tuned, 3D positions are preserved even as style is applied. The two goals do not interfere.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small experiment: take a 3D scene (e.g., a simple synthetic object or a real scene from a public dataset like CO3D). Render it from 4 different camera angles. Provide a style reference image (e.g., an oil painting or watercolor). Run Stylos on this input. Render the trained model from 8 new angles (angles the model never saw). Measure (1) how similar the style is across those 8 viewpoints (voxel coherence), and (2) how close the 3D shape stays to the original (RMSE of positions).
demo.metric_eq: voxel_coherence = 1 - (mean_squared_error of voxel features across viewpoints / variance of target style features); geometry_preservation_error = sqrt(mean((predicted_position - original_position)^2)) for all voxels
demo.closing: The demo must show that unseen viewpoints produce the same style (coherence near 1.0) and the shape error is small (preservation near 0.0), proving that the voxel loss and dual pathways work together.
